title: Don Geiss, America And Hope

jokes.text: Yeah, I'm supposed to be drinking a soda right now.
jokes.setup: Jack thanks everyone for taking time out of their busy schedules.
jokes.punchline: An employee's 'busy schedule' turns out to be drinking a soda — deflating any sense of importance.
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient deadpan understatement that sets the show's tone immediately. The economy is excellent — one line does the job. Not especially original but well-placed.

jokes.text: I don't know why you're wearing girls' pajamas, but I'm sure it's cultural.
jokes.setup: Jack thanks the Tokyo office employees for staying up late for the simulcast.
jokes.punchline: His 'cultural' excuse barely conceals condescension toward the Japanese employees' pajamas, played as a diplomatic non-insult that's clearly still an insult.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack Donaghy — the veneer of corporate diplomacy barely masking casual cultural dismissiveness. Strong character integration; this could only come from Jack. The structure of 'I don't know why X, but I'm sure it's Y' is a reliable format executed well here.

jokes.text: Not Seinfeld, Friends, E.R. exciting. More like 3D episodes of Merlin exciting.
jokes.setup: Jack calls the Kabletown acquisition 'an exciting time for NBC.'
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts his own hype by comparing it to a mediocre network fantasy show getting a gimmicky upgrade rather than NBC's golden era.
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional self-aware NBC comedy writing. The structure is perfect: establish the high bar (Seinfeld/Friends/ER), then crash it with a precise, obscure-enough-to-be-funny alternative (Merlin in 3D). The specificity of 'Merlin' is the key — a generic bad show wouldn't work as well. Highly quotable and captures NBC's real-world decline in one line. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: Even if it is from... Philadelphia. [audience member yells] Go Eagles!
jokes.setup: Jack calls Kabletown a great company with a dramatic pause before the city name.
jokes.punchline: A random employee in the audience is apparently from Philadelphia and immediately shouts 'Go Eagles!' — revealing that Jack's disdain for Philly is shared enough to be a known quantity but someone in the room is a loyalist.
jokes.explanation: Solid setup using Jack's theatrical pause before 'Philadelphia' as if it's a slur, then the immediate audience reaction is a fun subversion. The running city rivalry bit escalates well.

jokes.text: How did you even get a snowball?
jokes.setup: A Philly fan is agitated in the audience during the town hall meeting.
jokes.punchline: Jack's first response to being apparently hit with a snowball isn't outrage but genuine logistical confusion — implying the snowball is the absurd detail, not the act of throwing it.
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly economical. The joke isn't that someone threw a snowball — it's Jack's total deadpan focus on the impossible logistics of obtaining a snowball indoors. One line, perfectly timed, maximum absurdist payoff. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: Philly rules! Cheesesteaks! Bobby Clarke! Will Smith! Your town sucks.
jokes.setup: The city rivalry between Boston (Jack) and Philadelphia escalates.
jokes.punchline: The fan's defense of Philly includes Bobby Clarke (hockey legend), Will Smith (The Fresh Prince), and cheesesteaks, then immediately insults Jack's city — the combination of the specific mix of references is funny.
jokes.explanation: The list format (cheesesteaks + hockey player + Will Smith) is somewhat funny in its randomness, but the joke doesn't have great craft. It works more as escalation than as a well-constructed gag.

jokes.text: You do not want this argument, Lemon. Boston is the greatest city in the world.
jokes.setup: Liz says 'Boo' to Jack's pro-Boston stance.
jokes.punchline: Jack's absolute certainty that Boston is the greatest city, delivered with his trademark imperious authority — the comedy is entirely in his conviction.
jokes.explanation: Works primarily as character comedy — Jack's absolute authority applied to a petty city rivalry. The setup of Liz saying 'Boo' and him not even acknowledging it is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Boston cream pie. Boston Rob Mariano. Birthplace of Benjamin Franklin.
jokes.setup: Liz is listing things associated with Boston to defend it.
jokes.punchline: Benjamin Franklin was actually born in Boston but associated with Philadelphia — the joke is that Liz's triumphant historical claim is technically correct but will immediately be rebutted.
jokes.explanation: The list builds nicely, and including Boston Rob Mariano (Survivor) as a 'Boston thing' alongside cream pie and Benjamin Franklin is a funny tonal mismatch. The Franklin setup for the next line's punchline is solid structure.

jokes.text: Yeah, then he looked around, realized it sucked, and moved to Philadelphia!
jokes.setup: Liz claims Benjamin Franklin as a Boston achievement.
jokes.punchline: Jack reclaims the argument by turning Franklin into evidence that Boston is bad — if he was born there but chose Philly, that's a referendum on Boston.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed historical judo move — taking Liz's evidence and flipping it. Good economy and structure, though the character integration is moderate (any debate-savvy character could deliver this).

jokes.text: Oh, did you just whip a battery at me?
jokes.setup: The city rivalry has escalated, Jack already noted a snowball.
jokes.punchline: Now a battery has been thrown — escalating from snowball to battery, a famous Philadelphia sports crowd behavior (Philly fans notoriously threw batteries at J.D. Drew). Jack's casual tone about being assaulted is the cherry on top.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from snowball to battery is perfect — it references real Philly sports fan infamy (batteries at J.D. Drew) while maintaining Jack's impossibly calm demeanor. The callback payoff earns its score.

jokes.text: My apologies to our friends from the great city of Los Angeles. [01:21] Hey. Stop laughing. L.A. Rules. Michael Bay, freeways, Legoland.
jokes.setup: Jack apologizes to LA employees after the Boston/Philly war, seeming diplomatic.
jokes.punchline: The LA person immediately gets defensive and their best defense of LA is Michael Bay, freeways, and Legoland — an embarrassingly weak list.
jokes.explanation: A nice coda to the city rivalry gag — by including LA, the show gives a third punchline. Michael Bay, freeways, and Legoland as LA's best assets is great comic economy. The running gag lands its third beat.

jokes.text: And the earth into one of the top three planets in the universe.
jokes.setup: Jack eulogizes Don Geiss as having built GE into 'the greatest company on earth.'
jokes.punchline: He then extends the praise to cosmological scale — Geiss also built Earth into a top-three planet — delivered completely straight.
jokes.explanation: This is an exceptional joke. The structure is flawless: start with genuine corporate praise ('greatest company on earth'), which sets up the logical extension that immediately becomes absurd ('one of the top three planets in the universe'). The deadpan delivery, the specificity of 'top three' (not first!), and the sheer scope of the escalation make this an outstanding line. Strong candidate for best joke in the episode. Fully justifies 8.8+ craft score.

jokes.text: There will be an episcopal cryogenic freezing service open to all six sigma black belts and higher.
jokes.setup: Jack announces a memorial service for Don Geiss.
jokes.punchline: The service combines an Episcopalian religious ceremony with cryogenic freezing, and access is gated by corporate achievement level (Six Sigma black belt) — three absurd elements fused into one sentence.
jokes.explanation: The combination of religious ceremony + sci-fi technology + corporate hierarchy gatekeeping is quintessential 30 Rock absurdism. The specificity of 'six sigma black belts and higher' as the admission criteria is what elevates this from merely funny to exceptional. Three separate comic concepts seamlessly fused. Justifies 8.0.

jokes.text: That's the craziest thing I ever heard. Episcopal!
jokes.setup: Jack describes the cryogenic freezing service — obviously the weird part is the cryogenics.
jokes.punchline: The employee's objection is specifically to the religious denomination, not the sci-fi freezing — the misdirection of what's 'crazy' here is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Masterful misdirection. The audience expects an objection to the cryogenics — but the employee zeroes in on 'Episcopal' as the offensive part. This is perfect comic subversion of expectations with absolute economy (two words do the work). One of the tightest jokes in the episode. Justifies 8.4.

jokes.text: I would be remiss if I didn't honor our fallen leader with a song. This is for you, Dan Goose. ♪ Amazing ♪ ♪ gra-♪ [trails off]
jokes.setup: Kenneth announces he wants to honor Don Geiss with a song at the town hall.
jokes.punchline: He calls the dead man 'Dan Goose' (wrong name, wrong animal) and then only manages to sing 'Amazing gra-' before the scene ends — implying his tribute is interrupted or he doesn't know the lyrics.
jokes.explanation: The name mangling ('Dan Goose' instead of 'Don Geiss') is perfect Kenneth — earnest and completely wrong. The abrupt song cutoff compounds the comedy. Strong character integration; this is pure Kenneth Parcell behavior.

jokes.text: Kenneth begins singing 'Amazing Grace' but trails off almost immediately into silence after '♪ gra-♪'
jokes.setup: Kenneth interrupts the town hall to honor Don Geiss with a song.
jokes.punchline: He begins 'Amazing Grace' but appears to forget the words almost immediately, trailing off after 'gra-'.
jokes.explanation: The anticlimax of the interruptive song pledge collapsing into a single syllable is a beautifully structured visual/audio gag. Kenneth's total commitment to a performance he cannot deliver is quintessential character comedy. The timestamp gap between ♪ amazing ♪ [02:06] and ♪ gra-♪ [02:12] suggests a long, painful pause before he even gets there.

jokes.text: Well, you know that scene in Notting Hill where they have the romantic date in the garden? Well, I would have rather watched that terrible movie five times than have hung out with Wesley.
jokes.setup: Jenna asks how Liz's second date with Wesley went.
jokes.punchline: Liz invokes a romantic movie scene to set up what sounds like a sweet comparison — then reveals she'd rather endure the movie (which she calls terrible) repeatedly than spend more time with him.
jokes.explanation: Good structure — the Notting Hill setup sounds like it's going one direction, then pivots. Calling Notting Hill terrible while using it as the baseline for a horrible evening is a nice Liz Lemon character touch.

jokes.text: Well, this morning I was buying an advanced ticket for the Truffaut retrospective at the Anthology Film Archives— One for the 8:00 Hot Tub Time Machine.
jokes.setup: Liz starts explaining the highbrow reason she was at the theater this morning — a Truffaut retrospective.
jokes.punchline: Wesley finishes her sentence, revealing they were both buying tickets to Hot Tub Time Machine (and neither was at the art house film).
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured misdirection. The Truffaut setup signals Liz's intellectual pretensions, but the punchline (Hot Tub Time Machine) simultaneously deflates both characters and creates the 'fate' coincidence joke. The parallel embarrassment makes it richer.

jokes.text: Are we both seeing Hot Tub Time Machine tonight? How does this keep happening?
jokes.setup: Liz keeps randomly running into Wesley despite trying to avoid him.
jokes.punchline: They've now coincidentally bought tickets to the same lowbrow movie at the same time.
jokes.explanation: Extends the universe-keeps-throwing-them-together running gag with the added layer that the meeting point is Hot Tub Time Machine specifically, which undercuts any 'fate is romantic' reading.

jokes.text: If there is a god, Liz, I think that she... ugh... is trying to tell us something.
jokes.setup: Wesley is trying to make a point about the universe pushing them together.
jokes.punchline: He visibly struggles to say 'she' for God — a British conservative fighting the progressive pronoun, the 'ugh' being the tiny character moment.
jokes.explanation: A subtle, layered character joke — the 'ugh' before 'she' reveals Wesley's discomfort with a female God while he's simultaneously trying to be progressive. Good character integration and economy; the joke is in a single syllable.

jokes.text: I had a thing where I kept running into Michael Douglas. But then I realized it was just some old lady who lives in my building.
jokes.setup: Wesley says it's like the universe keeps pushing them together.
jokes.punchline: Liz's version of a 'universe keeps bringing us together' story is that she kept seeing Michael Douglas — except it was a random old lady she mistook for him repeatedly.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Liz Lemon joke. The absurdity of repeatedly mistaking an old lady for Michael Douglas is already funny, but the self-deprecating implication (Liz can't recognize her own neighbor) and the completely serious delivery push it further. Highly quotable, perfectly economical, deeply character-specific. Justifies 8.3.

jokes.text: Okay. Escaped exotic animal or did he swallow another firecracker?
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz 'we have a Tracy problem.'
jokes.punchline: Liz rattles off two specific, equally plausible Tracy disasters as her first guesses — implying these have happened before and she has a diagnostic flowchart.
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy — the specific Tracy possibilities (exotic animal, swallowed firecracker) are both plausible given the character and imply a history. 'Another firecracker' is the key word — the 'another' does tremendous work. High character integration for both Liz and Tracy.

jokes.text: I just got the call from a friend at Little Brown. The publishing house? No, the premier talent agency for black dwarves.
jokes.setup: Jack mentions 'Little Brown' and Liz asks 'the publishing house?'
jokes.punchline: Jack redefines it as a talent agency for black dwarves — the specificity of 'premier' implying it's a real, established institution in this world.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect misdirection. Liz's clarifying question sets up the audience to expect confirmation of the mundane answer. The complete non-sequitur of 'premier talent agency for black dwarves' plus the word 'premier' (implying it's the best of several such agencies) is absurdist gold. Economy is excellent. Justifies 8.2.

jokes.text: My addiction to prescription glasses.
jokes.setup: Tracy lists the embarrassing revelations in the tell-all book about him.
jokes.punchline: His first listed scandal is an addiction to prescription glasses — a completely mundane medical accessory treated as a shameful substance dependency.
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist Tracy joke — treating corrective eyewear as a dangerous addiction worthy of a tell-all book scandal is perfectly in character. The mundane specificity (prescription, not just any glasses) elevates it.

jokes.text: The fact that I suffer from attention deficit disor— Jack, your shoes are shiny.
jokes.setup: Tracy begins listing his book's revelations, including his ADD.
jokes.punchline: He trails off mid-sentence because he's distracted by Jack's shiny shoes — demonstrating his ADD in real time as proof of the diagnosis.
jokes.explanation: This is among the best constructed jokes in the episode. The form IS the content — Tracy diagnosing himself with ADD while simultaneously demonstrating it is structurally perfect. The interruption by 'Jack, your shoes are shiny' is both the punchline and the proof. Tight, character-specific, structurally brilliant. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: And worst of all, she revealed the fact that I've never cheated on my wife.
jokes.setup: Tracy builds toward his most scandalous book revelation.
jokes.punchline: The 'worst' revelation is that he's been faithful — inverting the expected scandal (cheating) into the actual scandal (being a good husband in showbiz).
jokes.explanation: Superb inversion. The escalating 'worst of all' setup primes the audience for a shocking infidelity — the complete reversal (faithfulness as the scandal) is both funny and surprisingly sharp commentary on celebrity culture. Strong structure and character integration. Justifies 8.4.

jokes.text: Your Ben & Jerry's flavor is called Adulteraisin.
jokes.setup: Liz pushes back on the idea that Tracy's infidelity is all for show.
jokes.punchline: Tracy has a Ben & Jerry's flavor named 'Adulteraisin' — a portmanteau of 'adultery' + 'raisin' (and the flavor Chunky Monkey-style) that confirms his carefully constructed cheater brand.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes of the episode. 'Adulteraisin' is a perfect portmanteau — it works phonetically, conceptually (adultery + raisin as a flavor), and it implies a whole absurd commercial reality where Tracy's infidelity brand has been monetized into an ice cream flavor. Highly quotable, exceptionally original, perfect economy. Fully justifies 9.0.

jokes.text: I start losing my endorsements, Angie's gonna be madder than a bat in a suitcase.
jokes.setup: Tracy explains why maintaining his cheater image matters financially.
jokes.punchline: His simile for Angie's anger is 'madder than a bat in a suitcase' — a completely original, vivid, and inexplicable comparison that sounds both unhinged and somehow perfect.
jokes.explanation: Tracy Jordan's non-sequitur similes are a signature comedic device, and 'madder than a bat in a suitcase' is an excellent example. The image is specific enough to be vivid yet absurd enough to delight. Strong character integration — only Tracy would say this. Justifies 8.5.

jokes.text: Gordon. Gordon. Gordon! Oh!
jokes.setup: Someone appears to be calling to Gordon — possibly a bat escape or animal incident implied by the transition.
jokes.punchline: The escalating calls and final 'Oh!' suggest physical chaos just off-screen.
jokes.explanation: Hard to score without visual context. Could be a bat-in-suitcase callback. As written in transcript, the comedy is minimal — the escalating name-calls are a standard sitcom beat. Scores low without visual payoff.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. You have a problem with the science of Hot Tub Time Machine? Not the time travel. It's the hot tub. You don't just turn one on, and it's immediately hot. I should know. I've been in a hot tub two times.
jokes.setup: Wesley and Liz are at a movie together.
jokes.punchline: Wesley's scientific objection to Hot Tub Time Machine is not the implausible time travel but the hot tub heating time — and his expert credentials are having been in one twice.
jokes.explanation: Classic pedantic British character comedy. The inversion of objecting to hot tub physics while accepting time travel is sharp. 'I should know, I've been in a hot tub two times' is both the deflation of his authority and a character revelation. Well-constructed escalation of absurdity.

jokes.text: Yeah. Seltzer and Mike and Ikes. What did you want? Popcorn? Yes. Popcorn? At the cinema?
jokes.setup: Liz expresses mild dissatisfaction with the movie snacks Wesley got.
jokes.punchline: Wesley acts as if wanting popcorn at a movie theater is a bizarre, unreasonable request — treating a universal cinema experience as exotic.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy using Wesley's insufferable Britishness — acting as though American cinema popcorn is somehow gauche. The repetition of 'Popcorn? At the cinema?' with escalating incredulity is well-executed.

jokes.text: It's like being in a Cathy cartoon that just won't end.
jokes.setup: Wesley is criticizing Liz's food obsession.
jokes.punchline: Comparing Liz's food focus to the Cathy comic strip (a notoriously dated, food-obsessed single-woman cartoon) is a specific, cutting insult that also reveals Wesley's surprisingly specific knowledge of American newspaper comics.
jokes.explanation: The Cathy reference is perfectly targeted — it's a culturally specific, slightly obscure insult that lands harder for those who know the comic strip. The added layer of a British man wielding Cathy as a weapon is its own joke.

jokes.text: Oh, my god, I want to smash your face.
jokes.setup: Wesley has called Liz's food obsession annoying and compared her to Cathy.
jokes.punchline: Liz's response to being insulted isn't a witty retort but raw, barely-contained violence — which is both disproportionate and very on-brand for Liz Lemon.
jokes.explanation: Solid reaction beat — Liz's violence-adjacent frustration response is character-appropriate. The economy is excellent but it's not an especially original joke.

jokes.text: So why are you in my phone as 'future husband,' and why am I in yours as 'future wife'?
jokes.setup: Wesley says he doesn't think they were meant to be together either.
jokes.punchline: Despite both claiming they're incompatible, they've each saved the other in their phone with matrimonial titles — undercutting their protestations.
jokes.explanation: Good ironic reveal — the phone contact names undercut both characters' stated positions simultaneously. Nice structure, decent character integration.

jokes.text: At least we'll always have Dr. Kaplan's recovery room. It was our Paris.
jokes.setup: Wesley and Liz are trying to accept that they're not meant to be.
jokes.punchline: The Casablanca reference ('We'll always have Paris') is applied to a surgical recovery room — the most unromantic possible location as the site of their formative connection.
jokes.explanation: Smart Casablanca parody — 'It was our Paris' applied to an anesthesia recovery room is a precise comic subversion. The formality of 'our Paris' framing contrasts perfectly with the mundane medical setting.

jokes.text: We brought good things to life. And bad things to Chinese rivers.
jokes.setup: Jack recounts GE's legacy in a confessional, citing the old 'We bring good things to life' slogan.
jokes.punchline: The slogan's positive flip side is environmental contamination of Chinese waterways — a dark, self-aware corporate admission.
jokes.explanation: Excellent dark corporate comedy. The direct callback to GE's actual famous ad slogan ('We Bring Good Things to Life') then immediately undermined with 'and bad things to Chinese rivers' is structurally elegant and politically sharp. Maximum economy — one additional clause does enormous work. Justifies 8.4.

jokes.text: Second only to the company of great friends.
jokes.setup: Jack has just said GE is a great company.
jokes.punchline: He pivots to an unexpectedly sentimental non-sequitur about friendship — absurdly out of character for Jack, who would never value friendship over corporate achievement.
jokes.explanation: Mild character irony — Jack expressing sentimentality is always slightly funny given his nature. Not particularly sharp or original.

jokes.text: My cousin in Atlanta is a business model. She holds up staplers in catalogues.
jokes.setup: Jack explains Kabletown has 'a whole different business model.'
jokes.punchline: Kenneth mishears 'business model' as the profession of modelling and volunteers that his cousin is one — she models office supplies.
jokes.explanation: Pure Kenneth joke — his literal-minded misinterpretation of 'business model' is very on-brand. 'She holds up staplers in catalogues' is the perfect specific detail. Good character integration and economy.

jokes.text: So I can prove that I am the man with the ambition, the talent, and the looking-at-my-watch skills to run this company.
jokes.setup: Jack explains he's meeting with an old colleague to learn about Kabletown.
jokes.punchline: His list of executive qualifications ends with 'looking-at-my-watch skills' — a ridiculous physical tic elevated to a core leadership competency.
jokes.explanation: Excellent list joke — the first two items (ambition, talent) are sincere, which sets up the absurdist third item as the payoff. 'Looking-at-my-watch skills' specifically implies a whole executive theater that's simultaneously meaningless and important-seeming. Good character integration.

jokes.text: So all we need you to do is put us under anesthesia again. Wesley brought his video camera. In England, we call it a film pod.
jokes.setup: Liz and Wesley are back at Dr. Kaplan's office asking for another anesthesia session.
jokes.punchline: Wesley's addition that he brought a 'film pod' (his word for video camera) adds a layer of absurdity to an already absurd request.
jokes.explanation: Functional absurdist comedy — the premise of seeking anesthesia for romantic clarity is already funny. 'Film pod' is a mild Wesley-ism.

jokes.text: My brother is a cardiologist and I'm just as good as he is. We drive the same car. So what if his wife is more attractive?
jokes.setup: Dr. Kaplan pushes back on being asked to do something unethical, asserting he's a real doctor.
jokes.punchline: His evidence that he's equal to his cardiologist brother is: same car, no acknowledgment that he buried his patient, and defensiveness about the wife's attractiveness — each detail revealing deep professional envy.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating character revelation — each detail about Dr. Kaplan's rivalry with his cardiologist brother adds a layer of insecurity. 'So what if his wife is more attractive?' is the perfect vulnerable cap to the escalation. Strong character comedy.

jokes.text: We are gonna hang out so much after this. I want to take you to the Big Apple Circus 'cause we're best friends.
jokes.setup: Dr. Kaplan shows Liz and Wesley footage of what they said in the recovery room.
jokes.punchline: Under anesthesia, Liz's deepest connection with Wesley was immediate, drug-fueled best-friend energy focused on the Big Apple Circus — not romance.
jokes.explanation: Funny in its specificity — not a generic 'let's be friends' but specifically the Big Apple Circus as the pinnacle of desired shared activity. The contrast between the romantic framing and the childlike enthusiasm works well.

jokes.text: And if my heart surgeon brother is so great, how come so many of his patients have died, but I've only killed one guy, huh?
jokes.setup: Dr. Kaplan continues defending himself after Liz and Wesley leave.
jokes.punchline: His defense of his medical record against his brother's is that he's only killed one patient — delivered as a point of pride, completely missing that any patient death is catastrophic.
jokes.explanation: Dark medical comedy with perfect character consistency. 'I've only killed one guy' as a brag is wonderfully bleak, and the competitive framing against his brother's mortality stats makes it a callback payoff. Justifies 8.0.

jokes.text: Say it ain't so, Tray. What about the Seattle Seahawks cheerleader? That one kind of thick Rockette? That blind woman in the business class bathroom on the Acela?
jokes.setup: Frank is devastated to learn Tracy has never cheated on his wife.
jokes.punchline: Frank's cherished catalog of specific Tracy infidelity lore includes these three specific, hilariously detailed alleged encounters — each more specific and degraded than the last.
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalating list — the specificity of 'that one kind of thick Rockette' and 'blind woman in the business class bathroom on the Acela' implies that Frank has treasured these stories like sacred texts. Strong character comedy and escalation.

jokes.text: I looked up to you. Now I hate you.
jokes.setup: Frank is processing that Tracy was always faithful.
jokes.punchline: Frank's rapid emotional reversal — from admiration to hatred based entirely on Tracy being a good husband — is a perfect encapsulation of the writer's room character.
jokes.explanation: Economy is exceptional — two short sentences do enormous character work. The moral inversion (hating someone for being good) is very funny, though not deeply original.

jokes.text: I got a lot of flack after I ate the pig that played Babe.
jokes.setup: A colleague is giving Tracy advice about managing PR scandals.
jokes.punchline: The 'flack' he received was for eating the celebrity pig — treating the consumption of a famous movie animal as a normal celebrity PR problem.
jokes.explanation: Dark, specific, and absurd — eating the actual Babe pig as a PR scandal is a wonderfully left-field reference. The matter-of-fact delivery as advice for Tracy makes it land better.

jokes.text: I'm here to announce that I'm leaving show business to spend more time with my stripper. But it's like a black Barbie doll in Arizona. Nobody's buying it.
jokes.setup: Tracy held a press conference to do damage control on the faithfulness revelation.
jokes.punchline: 'Leaving show business to spend more time with my stripper' as a cover story is already absurd, and 'like a black Barbie doll in Arizona, nobody's buying it' is a vividly specific metaphor for implausibility.
jokes.explanation: Two excellent jokes in one: the press conference statement ('leaving show business for my stripper') and the metaphor ('black Barbie doll in Arizona'). The simile is the standout — it's original, visual, and specific. Strong Tracy voice throughout. Justifies 8.0.

jokes.text: But John Edwards and I were supposed to ride on their Cinco de Mayo float.
jokes.setup: Tracy just lost the Horny Goat Weed endorsement.
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Tracy and John Edwards (who was at the time mired in an infidelity scandal) were scheduled to co-appear on a Cinco de Mayo float for a libido supplement is multi-layered absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Densely funny: Tracy + John Edwards (specific current-events reference to infidelity scandal) + Horny Goat Weed + Cinco de Mayo float = four comic elements stacked in one sentence. The specificity of all the details makes it exceptional. Justifies 8.2.

jokes.text: Yet another black superstar taken down by his personal life. Just like my favorite golfer, OJ Simpson.
jokes.setup: Tracy is lamenting his situation as a black celebrity undone by personal scandal.
jokes.punchline: He names OJ Simpson as his 'favorite golfer' — a dark joke combining OJ's post-murder-acquittal golf hobby, his race, and the scandal pattern Tracy invokes.
jokes.explanation: Dark and sharp — OJ's post-trial golf obsession is the specific comic hook that makes this more than a generic OJ joke. The frame of 'favorite golfer' is the perfect delivery mechanism. Good economy.

jokes.text: Remember how you tricked the owner of that toaster company into thinking you were his dead son? And he sold you the factory for $1.
jokes.setup: Jack is reminiscing with old colleague Dave about past business exploits.
jokes.punchline: Jack's nostalgic example of Dave's business genius is a deeply dark con — impersonating a dead child to steal a factory for a dollar.
jokes.explanation: Dark corporate backstory comedy — the sheer specificity and moral depravity of the scheme (tricking a grieving father, buying a company for $1) is presented as fond nostalgia. Good dark subversive comedy.

jokes.text: I was only as good as my mentor, the man who taught me how to bait the enemy, Jack 'the Master Baiter' Donaghy.
jokes.setup: Dave is crediting Jack for his business acumen.
jokes.punchline: 'The Master Baiter' is a pun on 'masturbator' delivered completely straight as a nickname, making it simultaneously a double entendre and a legitimate business title.
jokes.explanation: A classic double-entendre pun, well-delivered in context. The 'master baiter' pun isn't highly original but the setup (a business nickname) and the deadpan delivery work well enough to earn its score.

jokes.text: Oh, good god. Ass-atar. The Lovely Boners. The Hind Side. Based on the novel 'Tush' by Assfire.
jokes.setup: Dave is showing Jack Kabletown's most lucrative product — the pay-per-view porn channel.
jokes.punchline: Jack reads the titles of films on channels 500-600, which are all porn parody titles of real movies (Avatar, The Lovely Bones, The Blind Side, based on the novel Push by Sapphire).
jokes.explanation: Rapid-fire porn parody titles that each require unpacking: Ass-atar (Avatar), The Lovely Boners (The Lovely Bones), The Hind Side (The Blind Side), 'Tush' by Assfire (Push by Sapphire). The density is exceptional and each title is well-crafted. 'Based on the novel Tush by Assfire' is a particularly brilliant construction. High quotability. Justifies 8.3.

jokes.text: Do you know how much of our profit comes from men ordering adult movies? 91%.
jokes.setup: Dave reveals Kabletown's business model.
jokes.punchline: 91% of profit from pay-per-view porn — the comic specificity of the exact percentage (not 'most' but 91%) gives it a mock-statistical authority.
jokes.explanation: The precision of '91%' is the comic touch here — it has the feel of a real stat delivered absurdly. Functional setup joke for the larger Kabletown reveal.

jokes.text: Well, buying NBC counts as a charitable donation for tax purposes.
jokes.setup: Jack asks why Kabletown even wants NBC if they're profitable from porn.
jokes.punchline: NBC is such a failed network that acquiring it qualifies as a tax-deductible charitable donation — treating a major broadcast network as a charity case.
jokes.explanation: Devastating self-aware NBC joke. The idea that buying NBC is a charitable write-off is both commercially astute (NBC was genuinely struggling) and maximally self-deprecating. Perfect economy, great structure — the 'for tax purposes' addition is the perfect clinical kicker. One of the episode's best jokes. Justifies 8.7.

jokes.text: You're the classic American executive. You will look great standing behind our CEO at press conferences.
jokes.setup: Jack asks why Kabletown wants him specifically.
jokes.punchline: His value to Kabletown is purely decorative — he looks good as backdrop scenery at press conferences. The reduction of Jack Donaghy, master executive, to a prop.
jokes.explanation: Good character-targeted irony — Jack's entire identity is as a maker and mover, so being told he's valuable as scenery is the maximum insult to his ego. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: I went to Harvard Business School. I'm the reason the microwave tray rotates.
jokes.setup: Jack protests being told his role is decorative.
jokes.punchline: His evidence of his innovative genius is that he's personally responsible for the rotating microwave tray — a ubiquitous but utterly banal appliance feature.
jokes.explanation: Jack's specific, unironic pride in the rotating microwave tray is excellent character comedy. Following 'Harvard Business School' with 'microwave tray rotation' as his greatest achievement is a comic deflation that also reveals GE's actual product world. Highly quotable. Justifies 8.1.

jokes.text: 'And Alexander wept, for there were no more worlds to conquer.' Hans Gruber, Die Hard.
jokes.setup: Dave tells Jack not to fight it — Kabletown has the perfect business.
jokes.punchline: Jack quotes what sounds like a profound historical statement (Alexander the Great), but his attribution is to Hans Gruber from Die Hard rather than any historical source.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Jack Donaghy joke — the character who would quote Alexander the Great in a business meeting is the same character who would attribute it to a movie villain. The layers: the quote is real (Alexander the Great via Plutarch), Hans Gruber paraphrases it in Die Hard, and Jack cites Die Hard as the source — entirely in character for someone whose cultural references are filtered through corporate American masculinity. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific. Justifies 8.5.

jokes.text: Hey, I know you're off-duty, but is there any chance you would take me to the Upper West Side? [taxi stops] Oh, good catch. Thank you so much. OW.
jokes.setup: Liz hails an off-duty cab.
jokes.punchline: She thanks the driver for 'catching' her bag or something, then immediately says 'Ow' — implying she immediately walked into something or was hit in a physical comedy beat.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy bit that relies heavily on visuals we can only infer from the transcript. The 'Ow' payoff is functional but without the visual it's hard to assess. Likely stronger on screen.

jokes.text: Bloody hell! No, no, not again. That's not him, is it? [Wesley crashes into Liz on a bicycle] Gangway for footcycle!
jokes.setup: The running gag of Wesley and Liz coincidentally encountering each other.
jokes.punchline: Wesley crashes into Liz on a bicycle while yelling 'Gangway for footcycle!' — both the accidental collision and the ridiculous word 'footcycle' are punchlines.
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of the collision plus 'footcycle' (Wesley's absurd word for bicycle) are both funny. 'Footcycle' is a particularly good neologism — British-sounding enough to be plausible while being completely wrong. Good running gag continuation.

jokes.text: Stop calling it that. Yeah, fine, my velocipede.
jokes.setup: Liz objects to 'footcycle.'
jokes.punchline: Wesley's correction to 'velocipede' (an archaic Victorian word for bicycle) makes it even worse — he's choosing an even more obscure, more pretentious term.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'footcycle' to 'velocipede' is perfectly calibrated — Wesley's correction is worse than his original error and more revealing of his character. 'Velocipede' is a genuinely funny word and calling it out as Wesley's 'correction' shows sharp writing.

jokes.text: The universe wants us to settle for one another. / Settling soul mates? That is grim. / And I've played Monopoly alone.
jokes.setup: Wesley proposes they're 'settling soul mates' — fated to be together not through love but resignation.
jokes.punchline: Liz calls it 'grim,' then immediately provides her own evidence of desperation: playing Monopoly alone — which validates that she might indeed need to settle.
jokes.explanation: The 'settling soul mates' phrase is sharp, but 'And I've played Monopoly alone' is the gem — Liz self-owns so completely that it validates Wesley's point even as she objects. Perfect Liz Lemon character comedy. The self-awareness undercuts her protest beautifully. Justifies 8.2.

jokes.text: I could open jars and kill bugs for you, and you could make me look less gay at work functions.
jokes.setup: Wesley is making the practical case for their relationship.
jokes.punchline: His pitch for their mutual benefit is jar-opening and bug-killing (for her) vs. heterosexual beard duties (for him) — reducing marriage to the most transactional and unflattering possible terms.
jokes.explanation: Excellent comic construction — the asymmetry of 'jars and bugs' vs. 'covering my sexuality' escalates wonderfully. Both sides of the transaction are equally degrading in different ways. Wesley offering to 'look less gay' is a sharp character revelation. Good economy.

jokes.text: You wouldn't be complaining if you wore the shoes I bought you. / You're an old bitch.
jokes.setup: Wesley asks Liz to point to a couple that's actually in love.
jokes.punchline: The real couple Wesley indicates is mid-argument — 'You're an old bitch' delivered in the middle of a shoe dispute — meant to illustrate that all couples bicker.
jokes.explanation: Functional observational joke about couples fighting — the specific shoe grievance and the blunt 'old bitch' response are mildly funny but not distinguished. Works as a visual beat in context.

jokes.text: Grow old with me, Liz? In separate bedrooms? No way.
jokes.setup: Wesley makes a romantic entreaty for Liz to grow old with him.
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately clarifies his romantic proposal would require separate bedrooms — Wesley doesn't object to the separate bedrooms, just confirms it and she still rejects it.
jokes.explanation: Nice quick beat — the separate bedrooms assumption (not denied by Wesley) deflates any romantic pretense. Economical and functional.

jokes.text: You'd have someone to tell you when you're about to step in something. Ah, nerds!
jokes.setup: Wesley is selling Liz on the practical benefits of their relationship.
jokes.punchline: He finishes his pitch by demonstrating his usefulness — immediately warning her she's about to step in something — but she says 'Ah, nerds!' implying she's heard enough and/or already stepped in it.
jokes.explanation: Nice physical gag payoff — Wesley's warning works as a demonstration of the very thing he's selling, and 'Ah, nerds!' is Liz's frustrated expletive-substitute. Works better visually.

jokes.text: Lemon, I'm not in the mood to solve your lady problems or listen to a story about whatever escapee from the island of misfit toys you're currently dating.
jokes.setup: Liz asks Jack for a pep talk.
jokes.punchline: Jack dismisses her love life with 'escapee from the island of misfit toys' — a specific, cutting metaphor for the type of man Liz typically dates.
jokes.explanation: Sharp Jack line — 'island of misfit toys' is a specific, vivid, and apt metaphor for Liz's dating history. The full dismissal ('lady problems,' 'escapee from') shows Jack's particular brand of contemptuous affection. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: No, this is a Liz relationship emergency. It's a Liz-aster.
jokes.setup: Liz insists her situation is urgent.
jokes.punchline: 'Liz-aster' = 'Liz' + 'disaster' — a self-deprecating portmanteau that has the added layer of Liz coining her own personal disaster neologism.
jokes.explanation: Good portmanteau — 'Liz-aster' is cleverly self-aware and the fact that Liz has apparently coined it for herself implies this happens often. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Ever since I was little— No, faster than that. My whole adult life— No! Oprah says— You have ten seconds.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Liz to explain her problem.
jokes.punchline: Jack keeps truncating Liz's attempts to frame her story, cutting off each framing device (childhood origin story, adult context, Oprah-ism) until he imposes a 10-second limit.
jokes.explanation: Good escalating character beat — Jack's patience running out through Liz's increasingly elaborate narrative framings ('Oprah says' being the last straw) is very true to both characters.

jokes.text: Is it? Maybe you should settle. Everybody settles.
jokes.setup: Liz says a guy thinks she should settle for him and it's 'completely and totally wrong.'
jokes.punchline: Jack's immediate agreement that she should settle — delivered without irony — is both a character moment and a subversion of the expected 'you deserve better' response.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jack subversion — rather than the expected supportive response, he immediately validates the settling theory. This works because it's both cruel and possibly true. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: At one point, my obituary was going to read, 'CEO of G.E. dies violently in a casino orgy.'
jokes.setup: Jack is making the case that everyone settles, using himself as an example.
jokes.punchline: His previous aspirational obituary was death by casino orgy — presented as a professional goal that has since been lost.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Jack lines in the episode. 'CEO of G.E. dies violently in a casino orgy' as a life aspiration is perfectly specific, deeply character-appropriate (this IS Jack's ideal death), and shockingly dark. The specificity of 'violently' in a casino orgy is the cherry that makes it exceptional. Justifies 8.8.

jokes.text: 'Middle manager of a Philadelphia pornography distributor never wakes up.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks what his obituary will say now after the Kabletown deal.
jokes.punchline: The deflated version of his obituary — 'middle manager of a Philadelphia pornography distributor never wakes up' — captures his reduced status (middle manager), the shame of Kabletown's business, Philly callback, and a passive death.
jokes.explanation: The contrast with the casino orgy obituary makes this devastating. Every word is doing work: 'middle manager' (demotion), 'Philadelphia' (callback to the city rivalry and Kabletown shame), 'pornography distributor' (the business reality), 'never wakes up' (the anticlimactic passive death vs. 'dies violently'). This is the episode's comic peak and one of the best jokes in the transcript. Fully justifies 8.9.

jokes.text: Maybe it is the perfect business. A perpetual motion machine endlessly satisfying every human need.
jokes.setup: Liz accidentally defends the Kabletown model.
jokes.punchline: Jack picks up on 'sounds pretty good' and starts earnestly philosophizing about porn distribution as a perpetual motion machine — his corporate brain re-engaging with what he'd been resisting.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Jack's intellectual engagement with the porn business is funny because he can't help himself. The 'perpetual motion machine' framing applied to PPV porn is good comedy.

jokes.text: I'm going to bury Don Geiss, America, and hope.
jokes.setup: Jack is having an emotional realization that Kabletown doesn't need what he offers.
jokes.punchline: He declares he's going to 'bury Don Geiss, America, and hope' — conflating a literal funeral with the death of his professional ambitions and entire national optimism.
jokes.explanation: The escalating list structure — from a person (Geiss) to a country (America) to a concept (hope) — is both genuinely affecting and funny in its grandiosity. The episode title payoff makes it a standout line with meta significance.

jokes.text: I saw some women came forward to say you didn't have sex with them.
jokes.setup: Jenna checks in on Tracy's scandal situation.
jokes.punchline: Women are coming forward to confirm the absence of an affair — the PR inverse of typical celebrity scandal where women confirm the presence of an affair.
jokes.explanation: Sharp inversion of celebrity scandal conventions — women coming forward to deny sleeping with Tracy is the perfect satirical response to real-world scandal culture. Economical and well-constructed.

jokes.text: Somebody leaked my voicemails. 'Hey baby, it's your husband. So I'm at Bed Bath & Beyond and I can't remember, did you say to get metal or wood shower curtain rings? Oh, you're calling me on the other line. I can't wait to talk to you. I love you.'
jokes.setup: Tracy's faithful husband scandal is escalating.
jokes.punchline: The leaked 'scandalous' voicemail is a completely mundane domestic call — shopping for curtain rings, excited to take her call — which is devastating to his bad-boy brand but adorable in reality.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. The voicemail is meticulously crafted — Bed Bath & Beyond, curtain ring specificity (metal vs. wood), the genuine excitement about her calling back — all of it building a portrait of a devoted husband that perfectly inverts Tracy Jordan's public persona. 'I can't wait to talk to you' is the killer detail. Justifies 8.5.

jokes.text: She says I better have an affair and quick before it tears our family apart.
jokes.setup: Liz asks how Angie feels about the faithfulness revelation.
jokes.punchline: Angie's response is to demand Tracy have an affair immediately to save their marriage — the complete inversion of normal domestic logic.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding absurdist inversion — the wife demanding the husband cheat to save the marriage is a logical extension of the episode's premise taken to its extreme. The economy is excellent and the character logic (for Angie and Tracy's world) is impeccable. Justifies 8.3.

jokes.text: I wish I could help you, but I can't sleep with a black guy. I'd lose my endorsement deal with NASCAR.
jokes.setup: Tracy needs someone to sleep with him to save his career.
jokes.punchline: Jenna's refusal is framed not as moral but contractual — her NASCAR sponsorship prohibits interracial sex, treating institutional racism as a business arrangement.
jokes.explanation: Dark and sharp — the NASCAR-as-racism-enforcer joke is uncomfortable but the framing (contractual rather than personal) is the satirical point. Jenna's matter-of-fact delivery of her own racism as a business constraint is perfectly in character. Justifies 8.0.

jokes.text: Hello, Elizabeth. May I offer you a succulent fruit? [15:30] Let me do a dance for you, my lover.
jokes.setup: Tracy has decided to try to seduce Liz to save his career.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's seduction attempt involves formal address ('Hello, Elizabeth'), offering fruit, and promising a dance — the maximum awkward formality of a man who has no game outside his public persona.
jokes.explanation: Funny in its formality — 'succulent fruit' and 'my lover' are hilariously inappropriate coming from Tracy. The scene plays well on the cringe of the attempted seduction.

jokes.text: I can't have sex with you, Liz Lemon. I love Angie too much.
jokes.setup: Tracy has been doing a seductive dance for Liz.
jokes.punchline: Tracy pulls back from his own seduction by invoking the love that's the source of all his problems — the faithfulness as both the problem and its own solution.
jokes.explanation: Good character payoff — Tracy's inability to cheat reasserts itself even in the moment of attempted infidelity. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: You know what I have? A Sims family that keeps getting murdered.
jokes.setup: Liz tells Tracy to be grateful for his stable family life, listing what she lacks.
jokes.punchline: Her equivalent of Tracy's devoted family is a Sims household that keeps dying — implying either bad luck or that she's actively killing them, both of which are funny.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode, possibly the series. 'A Sims family that keeps getting murdered' is exceptional on every level: perfectly character-specific (Liz would both have a Sims family and be incapable of keeping them alive), the word 'murdered' vs. 'died' implies agency (is she doing it?), and it perfectly encapsulates her loneliness through an absurd specific detail. Highly quotable, deeply original. Fully justifies 9.0.

jokes.text: One day you will have what I have because you're an amazing, strong, and intelligent woman like Hilary... from Fresh Prince of Bel-Air.
jokes.setup: Tracy tries to give Liz an inspirational compliment in return for her pep talk.
jokes.punchline: He starts with sincere flattery, implying a great woman comparison — then his reference point is Hilary Banks from Fresh Prince, the most shallow, airheaded character on that show.
jokes.explanation: Perfect misdirection — 'amazing, strong, intelligent woman' sets up a meaningful comparison, but the beat before 'from Fresh Prince' builds anticipation, and Hilary Banks (defined by being vain and frivolous) as the destination is Tracy-perfect. The clarification 'from Fresh Prince of Bel-Air' is essential and funny on its own. Justifies 8.2.

jokes.text: Ugh! I'm sorry. I was still riding the vibe from earlier.
jokes.setup: Tracy says something nice to Liz and then apparently does something weird/inappropriate.
jokes.punchline: His apology for whatever physical or verbal thing he did ('riding the vibe from earlier' — the seduction attempt) acknowledges that the seduction energy bled into the sincere moment.
jokes.explanation: Functional callback joke — 'riding the vibe from earlier' is funny character language. Works better with the visual of whatever Tracy did. Moderate craft.

jokes.text: I'll never forget the first thing he ever said to me. 'These are all hookers. Pick one.' Then after we picked our hookers and the plane took off, he told me his business philosophy.
jokes.setup: Jack eulogizes Don Geiss at the memorial service.
jokes.punchline: Geiss's first words to Jack were about selecting from a lineup of sex workers on a plane — presented as a formative mentorship memory, the dark detail of 'Then after we picked our hookers' being treated as a perfectly normal preamble to a business lesson.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional dark comedy. The eulogy format makes the revelation more shocking. 'Then after we picked our hookers and the plane took off' is delivered as the most normal transitional clause imaginable. The move from sex workers to business philosophy as a fluid narrative is perfectly structured. Justifies 8.3.

jokes.text: Don was the one who realized there was a whole segment of consumers not buying light bulbs. The asleep. That realization led him to develop the nightlight and the marketing campaign aimed at making children afraid of the dark — a monster under every bed.
jokes.setup: Jack is praising Don Geiss's business innovations.
jokes.punchline: Geiss's genius was identifying sleeping people as an untapped light bulb market, developing nightlights, and then deliberately traumatizing children with monster mythology to create demand — presented as admirable innovation.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The satirical logic is immaculate: identify untapped market (sleeping people) → create product (nightlight) → manufacture the need through deliberate childhood psychological trauma (monsters). 'A monster under every bed' as a corporate marketing campaign delivered admiringly at a eulogy is devastatingly funny and sharp corporate satire. Justifies 8.8.

jokes.text: That realization led him to develop the nightlight and the marketing campaign aimed at making children afraid of the dark -- a monster under every bed.
jokes.setup: Don Geiss discovered sleeping people as an untapped market.
jokes.punchline: His solution — deliberately manufacturing childhood fear to sell nightlights — is presented as brilliant business innovation in a solemn eulogy.
jokes.explanation: Masterful dark comedy. The corporate logic of manufacturing fear to create demand for your product — nightlights — is a devastating satire of marketing. 'A monster under every bed' as the campaign tagline presented admiringly at a funeral is peak 30 Rock. The satirical target (predatory marketing to children) is handled with absolute deadpan commitment.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. But I just had an amazing business idea. You'll have to excuse me.
jokes.setup: Jack is mid-eulogy for Don Geiss.
jokes.punchline: He interrupts his own eulogy to chase a business idea — Don Geiss's spirit apparently inspired an immediate pivot away from grieving.
jokes.explanation: The eulogy interruption is perfectly Jack — he literally honors Don Geiss by immediately doing what Don Geiss would have done. The meta-tribute is unintentional but poetic. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Gentlemen, there is a giant segment of consumers who are not buying our most lucrative product. Three words: Porn for women.
jokes.setup: Jack has a business revelation inspired by Geiss's nightlight insight.
jokes.punchline: 'Three words: Porn for women' — applying the untapped market logic to women's viewing habits, the reveal being that 'porn for women' isn't what they think.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for what follows. The 'three words' construction is classic comedy (the number doesn't match in expected ways — it's technically three words but the punch is in the concept). Strong setup for the subsequent explanation.

jokes.text: Jack, women hate porn almost as much as men hate going to outlet malls.
jokes.setup: Jack pitches porn for women.
jokes.punchline: The executive's objection includes an unexpectedly specific male grievance (outlet mall hatred) as the comparative measure for female porn aversion.
jokes.explanation: Functional joke — the outlet mall comparison is a specific, recognizable male resentment. Not exceptional but good supporting comedy.

jokes.text: But women do have one insatiable need. To jabber. And it doesn't matter if you have a headache or you're not in the mood... they barge right into your office and start complaining about a boyfriend or a coworker. And you're supposed to sit there and nod and tell them they're right. And the more you give it to them, the more they want it.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining his 'porn for women' concept.
jokes.punchline: His entire description of women's 'insatiable need to jabber' is a sustained double entendre applying porn viewing metaphors (doesn't matter if you have a headache, the more you give it to them) to emotional conversation — his genuine sexism framed as business insight.
jokes.explanation: Sustained double-entendre comedy — Jack's description of women wanting to talk uses porn-viewer language ('headache,' 'more they want it') while describing emotional intimacy needs. The irony that his 'porn for women' is just men listening is the satirical point. Good character integration.

jokes.text: I'll tell you, sometimes my wife will be blathering on about something, and I'll think: I'm more than just a pair of ears. You know, I'm a person who thinks about sex every seven seconds.
jokes.setup: The executive is relating to Jack's description of women wanting to talk.
jokes.punchline: The executive's response to being treated as 'just a pair of ears' is to assert his personhood through the cliché of thinking about sex every seven seconds — a deeply ironic choice of dignity claim.
jokes.explanation: Good supporting character moment — 'I'm more than just a pair of ears, I'm a person who thinks about sex every seven seconds' is a funny self-undermining dignity claim.

jokes.text: I'll tell you, sometimes my wife will be blathering on about something, and I'll think, 'I'm more than just a pair of ears. You know, I'm a person who thinks about sex every seven seconds.'
jokes.setup: The executives are understanding Jack's pitch through personal experience.
jokes.punchline: The executive identifies with being used just for listening — and his assertion of personhood is that he thinks about sex every seven seconds.
jokes.explanation: Good use of the 'sex every seven seconds' statistic as a complaint about being reduced to a listening device. The reversal of victimhood (men are also objects!) in the context of the pitch is funny. Functional supporting character comedy.

jokes.text: So what if women had a pay-per-view channel featuring handsome men patiently listening to them? What if they had... Porn for women?
jokes.setup: Jack has been building to the reveal of his 'porn for women' concept.
jokes.punchline: The 'porn for women' is literally men listening patiently — the anti-porn, the most mundane possible 'fantasy' elevated to pornographic status.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the setup — men listening as female pornography is a sharp gender-satirical observation. The dramatic callback of 'Porn for women?' lands the setup well.

jokes.text: Don't you see this is just gonna keep happening? You can't fight the universe. / No, this isn't a coincidence. I wanted to see you, and I figured you wouldn't miss a tasting of the white wines of Scotland.
jokes.setup: Wesley encounters Liz again at what appears to be a very specific event.
jokes.punchline: Liz reveals she deliberately sought him out, correctly predicting he'd be at 'a tasting of the white wines of Scotland' — a hilariously pretentious and very Wesley-specific thing to attend.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — 'the white wines of Scotland' is a deeply specific, absurd event that perfectly characterizes Wesley (most restaurants refuse to serve them, suggesting they're terrible). Liz knowing he'd be there shows both her knowledge of him and the joke's consistency.

jokes.text: Most restaurants refuse to serve them.
jokes.setup: Liz mentions the white wines of Scotland event.
jokes.punchline: Wesley's defensive/proud clarification that most restaurants refuse to serve Scottish white wines implies they're terrible — but he attends tastings of them anyway.
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — the aside about restaurants refusing to serve Scottish white wine implies they're objectively bad, making Wesley's attendance at their tasting a character revelation. Efficient and well-placed.

jokes.text: Oh, yeah, you've only told me that, like, nine times.
jokes.setup: Wesley mentions most restaurants refuse to serve Scottish whites, apparently for the ninth time.
jokes.punchline: Liz's casual 'nine times' count reveals they've spent enough time together for repetitive Wesley-isms to accumulate — undercutting her claim that she doesn't want to see him.
jokes.explanation: Functional callback/running gag acknowledgment. The 'nine times' specificity is a mild laugh — it reveals the unshown history of their interactions. Not exceptional but functional.

jokes.text: Are you ready to settle and become Mrs. Snipes?
jokes.setup: Wesley asks if Liz has come around to settling.
jokes.punchline: He reveals his surname — 'Snipes' — which is the same as action star Wesley Snipes. The name 'Wesley Snipes' on a pale, insufferable British man is inherently absurd.
jokes.explanation: The Wesley Snipes name reveal is excellent — the show has been holding this back and the delivery as 'Mrs. Snipes' gives it maximum impact. A British twit named Wesley Snipes is inherently funny, and the extended bit that follows makes it even better. Justifies 8.0.

jokes.text: That is insane! No, it's insane that the actor Wesley Snipes has that name. If you saw a picture of him and a picture of me, and you were asked, 'who should be named Wesley Snipes?' You'd pick the pale Englishman every time.
jokes.setup: Liz reacts with shock to Wesley's surname being Snipes.
jokes.punchline: Wesley argues with complete conviction that the name 'Wesley Snipes' more naturally belongs to a pale Englishman than to the actual Wesley Snipes — 'Every time, Liz. Every time.'
jokes.explanation: Outstanding joke. Wesley's absolute conviction that the name 'Wesley Snipes' belongs to him, not the action star, is perfectly constructed — the logic is absurd but internally consistent. 'Every time, Liz. Every time.' is the perfect button. The character specificity (only this insufferable, self-certain Brit would argue this) is flawless. One of the episode's very best. Justifies 8.8.

jokes.text: Frankly, you should be having this conversation with him. Yeah, I'm gonna go do that.
jokes.setup: Wesley argues that Wesley Snipes the actor should explain why he took 'his' name.
jokes.punchline: Liz agrees and says she's going to go confront the actual Wesley Snipes — treating this insane premise as actionable.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation — Liz going along with the premise and deciding to actually confront Wesley Snipes the actor extends the joke into action. The 'I'm gonna go do that' is a great commitment gag.

jokes.text: I give you two months before you give up and decide to settle! I'll see you in May! For sweeps! That's what we call spring cleaning in England.
jokes.setup: Wesley shouts after Liz as she leaves.
jokes.punchline: Wesley predicts they'll meet in May 'for sweeps' — a television industry term for ratings periods — then tries to cover with 'That's what we call spring cleaning in England.' The meta-reference to TV sweeps is a 30 Rock self-aware joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta joke — Wesley accidentally uses the TV industry term 'sweeps,' then immediately tries to cover it with a fake English usage. The self-aware breaking of the fourth wall is perfectly executed and 'That's what we call spring cleaning in England' is a delightful cover story. Justifies 8.4.

jokes.text: 'Cause I'll just listen patiently and say things like, 'Uh-huh,' 'How annoying,' 'She's clearly jealous of you,' and 'Well, it's his loss.' You're a great woman. You deserve a great man. For just $24.95 an hour.
characters: TV Actor / Porn for Women channel
jokes.setup: Jack's 'Porn for Women' channel is shown in action — a handsome man speaking directly to camera.
jokes.punchline: The channel delivers exactly what was promised: a man performing active listening clichés, affirming the viewer, then the '$24.95 an hour' price tag.
jokes.explanation: Strong payoff to Jack's pitch — the specific listening clichés ('She's clearly jealous of you') are perfectly chosen, and the '$24.95 an hour' price tag perfectly mirrors actual pay-per-view pricing. The callback lands the episode's B-plot satisfyingly.

jokes.text: Yes, please. / It's the yellow button, sweetie.
jokes.setup: A woman is watching the 'Porn for Women' channel.
jokes.punchline: The woman is genuinely engaged — 'Yes, please' — and the actor tells her where the subscribe button is ('the yellow button, sweetie'), completing the porn-subscription metaphor with a caring instruction.
jokes.explanation: Good closing tag — 'Yes, please' as the viewer response to being listened to, and 'It's the yellow button, sweetie' as a tenderly delivered pay-per-view subscription prompt, is a satisfying episode button. The 'sweetie' is the final touch.

tmdb_overview: Jack needs to reestablish himself within the new corporate structure. Liz and Wesley continually run into each other, making them consider fate's role in their lives. Tracy's nanny writes an exposé.
insight: Season 4's densest episode delivers 61 jokes in pure character-comedy mode.
